line: Look around, it's allowed. The board has everything on it, mostly in my handwriting. Are you any good with fourteen-year-olds?
Because I have a job for anyone who says yes. Mostly it's glue. Do you live nearby?
Then you're five minutes from here and ten from the library. Those are my two places. Most of the kids only know one of them.
Lantern night. Ruth Hale and I are doing Diwali lanterns at the library. Kids from here, kids from her homework club, one table, far too much glue.
If it's here, only our kids come. If it's there, everybody's kids come, and ours get to be the experts for one evening. $ They stand up straighter. I've watched it happen.

Some people would rather. Mr. Deshpande has kept this hall going for twenty-five years, and he has his reasons. I just like watching a kid explain Diwali to his soccer friends, get half the story wrong, and nobody minds.
Hi, are you here for the youth program? No? Sorry. Meena Krishnan. I run the youth program and, lately, most of the association. The rest of the week I teach ESL at Lincoln Middle.
choice3: I'd rather not get roped in.

line: Sorry, are these chairs yours? No? Then I'm taking them. Meena Krishnan, from the youth program at the India Association hall.
I'm borrowing furniture for Thursday. Ruth says yes to everything. It's slightly alarming.
Morning. Give me one second, I'm writing something down before I forget it.
One of my students translated his dad's apartment lease. He's twelve. They got their security deposit back.
I gave him extra credit, which he didn't care about. He cared that the landlord said thank you, young man.
All the time. Kids translate the gas bill, the doctor, the parent-teacher conference about themselves. That last one is a problem.
choice2: I did that as a kid.

line: You can guess how the translation goes. Teacher says I'm doing great. So I call the parents with an interpreter on speaker. It's slower. It's honest.
Morning! Hold this for me? _hands you a ring of keys_ Eleven keys. I know what nine of them open.
choice1: Why do you have all the keys?
choice3: Here you go. I'll see you later.

line: Somebody wants the hall on Saturday for a baby's first birthday, the clinic wants it on Monday for flu shots, and the library wants our chairs. I said yes, yes and yes.
choice3: I'll let you sort it out.

line: Me, apparently. I said I'd run the association for one year. That was three years ago. Mr. Deshpande still does the roof and the numbers, and he tells me when I've said yes to too many things.

He's usually right about the numbers. I'm usually right about the people. $ He thinks the flu shots will bring strangers into the hall. I think that's what a hall is for. We'll see who's tired by Monday.
Morning. You're early. Good, I need hands. These boxes go behind the stage before nine.
The youth program's glue, paper and one very old tambourine. The board meets on Thursdays, and Mr. Deshpande likes the hall clear for it.
choice3: There. I'll let you set up.

line: He runs the association, and he runs it carefully. Every program here is a line in his budget. The youth program is one line. I make it go a long way.
I don't fight him. I just run half the program at the library, where nobody needs a board to approve a glue stick. He knows. He signs the budget anyway. $ [warm] That's how we work. It works.
Hi! You're just in time. Can you hold that door?
I'm borrowing the big tables for Thursday. Ruth says yes to everything. It's slightly alarming.
She is. She also labels everything. Look, this one says TABLE 4, DO NOT REMOVE. I'm removing it.
She wrote the label. She'll mind for one minute. When I started the youth program, the library was the first place that called me back.
The hall was already mine. The library I had to ask. Okay, you take that end.
{playerName}, a question. Do you have five minutes?
I've seen you at the hall and at the library. You talk to people the same way in both.
choice3: I'll take that as a compliment. See you.

line: More than you'd think. Most of the grown-ups have one voice for here and one for there. The kids notice.

Of course. Mine changes on the bus. $ You go from {homeLanguage} with the aunties to English with the library people and nobody has to slow down for you. That's a gift. The kids need to see someone do it without making a speech about it.
That's the right answer either way. Tuesdays, four to six. I'll find you a job. I always find a job.
Perfect timing. Are you free Thursday evening?
Lantern night at the library. I need someone at the table between our kids and Ruth's homework club, keeping the glue moving. Will you?
Because for the first twenty minutes they sit apart, every time. Someone in the middle passing glue gets them talking. It's very scientific.
Sorry, I'm on the phone between classes. Two of my students didn't come to school on Monday.
choice2: I'll let you make your calls.

line: I think so. Their parents heard about checks near the bus depot, and they kept everyone home.
Spent my prep period calling homes. One mother answered on the sixth try.
She asked if the school gives addresses to anyone. I told her what our policy says, which is no. She asked if I was sure. I said I'd find out in writing.
choice3: I hope you get an answer.

line: I've emailed the district lawyer. He takes about a week. Meanwhile I'm sending homework home with a cousin. $ [guarded] These rules split one classroom into the kids who come and the kids who stay home. I don't think that's an accident.
Hi. Good news from the district, if I can get anybody to use it.
They'll book interpreters for parent nights now, in person or by phone, if a family asks a week ahead.
Whatever they need. Tamil, Gujarati, Punjabi, Dari. The list is long.
Now I have to get the parents to ask. Asking a week ahead means admitting you need it, and a lot of fathers won't.
choice1: I can help spread the word.

line: I'm putting it on the board here and on the library's board, in six languages. Then I'll stand next to it. $ [warm] Honestly, it feels like progress. This is what it looks like when a country decides everybody's parents count.
choice1: I'll stand next to it with you.

line: You're at the hall a lot. I'm glad.
Not for the older ones. For someone your age, a bit. The young ones come for the festivals and the food.
I come for the kids, Tuesdays and Saturdays. And for the chai, I won't lie.
The library, Thursdays. Come Thursday too, if you like. Don't let this be the only door you use.
Mr. Deshpande built this place. I wouldn't be doing any of this without it. We like different doors, that's all. That's as much as I'll say inside the building he bought.
Ruth says you're a library regular now.
Good. It's a good library. Bring some of it back here, would you?
The kids here want to know what's over there. The ones in the homework club come back with library cards and look very grown-up.
Some don't know they're allowed. One girl thought you had to pay. I took six of them in March. Cards in ten minutes. Now one of them helps Ruth on Saturdays.
choice1: I'll try to bring some back.

line: Hello. I'm in the middle of something.
choice1: I owe you an apology for last time.

line: Thank you. It happens. Help me move a table sometime and we're even.
Not today, I'm grading forty essays called 'My Summer.' Three of them are about the same water park.
